title: Lincoln County CO well depth and costs
meta_description: Lincoln County well depths center around 54 ft, with most under 100 ft. Learn what that means for drilling cost, yields, and water levels here.
h1: Water wells in Lincoln County, Colorado
intro_html: Lincoln County sits on the eastern plains, and the well records here look different than the foothills or mountains. The state shows 4,063 well permits on file, with 2,689 reporting a total depth and 572 giving an actual pump test. That is enough data to get a realistic picture of how deep you are likely to drill, how much water you can expect, and what a new well will cost on land outside places like Limon, Arriba, Genoa, and Hugo.

sections.heading: Typical well depths in Lincoln County
sections.html:
Across Lincoln County, the median well depth is 54 feet. The middle half of wells run from 35 to 100 feet, and 73% of wells are under 100 feet total depth. Another 25% fall between 100 and 300 feet, with only 2% between 300 and 600 feet and essentially none deeper than 600 feet. The deepest on record reaches 1,320 feet, but that is an outlier.

For bidding, those numbers tell a driller they are more often punching a relatively shallow Ogallala, alluvial, or fractured-bedrock well on the plains. Expect quotes built around that 35–100 foot band, with some contingency if you are on higher ground or farther from existing wells.

sections.heading: How much water Lincoln County wells produce
sections.html:
Yield reports here are better than many rural counties. From 572 wells with pump tests, the median yield is 10.0 gpm, and the middle half fall between 6.0 and 15.0 gpm. Only 1% of tested wells came in under 1 gpm, while 17% are in the 1–5 gpm range. The bulk, 55%, produce 5–15 gpm, and 27% show 15+ gpm.

For a single household, 10 gpm is more than adequate under Colorado’s exempt domestic rules. On stock wells, that spread explains why some ranch setups can run multiple tanks off one well while others need careful rotation or storage tanks to even out supply.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend on the plains
sections.html:
Where static water levels are reported, the median depth to water is 35 feet, with the middle half between 21 and 105 feet. That means many wells hit water fairly shallow, but there are pockets where it sits a lot deeper. Looking over time, the median static level was 53 feet in the 1960s, 36 feet in the 2010s, and 35 feet so far in the 2020s.

Those decade medians do not point to a clear county‑wide decline. Instead, they suggest a reasonably stable water table in the main aquifers, though individual wells in fractured bedrock can still behave unpredictably, especially away from the Ogallala and alluvial zones.

sections.heading: Who drills here and how the well use breaks down
sections.html:
Lincoln County’s permits go back at least to the 1950s, with 59 from that decade, then 150 in the 1960s and 280 in the 1970s. Activity picked up with 322 in the 1980s and peaked at 681 in the 1990s. The 2000s saw 544 permits, the 2010s had 518, and there are already 173 on the books for the 2020s, with the newest in 2025.

About 59% of wells are for stock, 33% for domestic or household use, and 8% for irrigation. Most are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers (3,516 wells), with 261 in the Ogallala and 97 in alluvium. Eastwood Drilling, Hamacher Well Works Inc, and drillers listed as Authorized (Pe, Pg) show up most often in the records.

sections.heading: Drilling and complete well costs in Lincoln County
sections.html:
The ground here is mostly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, so drilling is straightforward compared to hard mountain granite. Typical drilling rates run about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 54‑foot median depth, the drilled hole alone pencils out around $1,900–$3,000.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house or stock system, and electrical, a finished well at that depth generally comes in somewhere around $7,900–$15,000. Deeper locations in the 100–300 foot range will scale those numbers up linearly by the extra footage, plus some added pump cost.

sections.heading: Environmental and water-quality risks to check
sections.html:
State mapping shows 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles somewhere in the county. That does not mean a given rural well is contaminated, but it is a flag to run lab testing on a new purchase, especially near known sites or along major highways.

Most wells are in fractured bedrock or the Ogallala, which can move contaminants differently than shallow alluvium. Standard bacteria, nitrate, and metals tests are a baseline; if you are close to mapped PFAS work, talk with your tester about adding that panel. Also leave room on the site for a compliant septic layout that will not crowd the well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Lincoln County lot
sections.html:
With 73% of wells under 100 feet and a 10.0 gpm median yield, the odds favor getting a workable domestic well on a typical rural parcel here. Still, you should pull nearby well permits and logs, especially around Hugo, Limon, Arriba, or Genoa, to see actual depths and yields on neighboring land.

Confirm what use your permit will allow: many rural parcels rely on exempt household or stock wells, and irrigation is more tightly controlled. Check that there is room for both a well and a septic system meeting current setbacks. If no well exists yet, budget at least the median‑depth cost range and make sure your purchase contract addresses what happens if drilling hits low yield.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Lincoln County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Lincoln County, the median well depth is 54 feet. The middle half of wells are between 35 and 100 feet deep, and 73% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. About 25% run from 100 to 300 feet, and only 2% are in the 300–600 foot range. The deepest well on record reaches 1,320 feet, but that is an exception, not the norm for most properties.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Lincoln County?
faq.a: From the 572 wells with reported pump tests, the median yield in Lincoln County is 10.0 gpm. The middle half are between 6.0 and 15.0 gpm. Only 1% of wells test under 1 gpm, while 17% fall in the 1–5 gpm range. Most wells perform better than that: 55% produce 5–15 gpm, and 27% test at 15 gpm or more, which is strong for domestic use.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Lincoln County?
faq.a: Based on reported static water levels, the median depth to water is 35 feet, with a middle half from 21 to 105 feet. By decade, the median was 53 feet in the 1960s, 36 feet in the 2010s, and 35 feet in the 2020s. Those medians suggest a generally stable county‑wide water level over time, though individual wells can behave differently depending on the specific aquifer and location.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Lincoln County, CO?
faq.a: Drilling in Lincoln County typically runs about $35–$55 per foot in the local alluvium and plains sedimentary formations. At the county’s 54‑foot median depth, the borehole cost is roughly $1,900–$3,000. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $7,900–$15,000 at that depth, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Lincoln County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Records show 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles in parts of the county, so testing matters. Before drinking from any private well, you should run at least bacteria, nitrate, and metals tests, and consider PFAS testing if you are near mapped sites. Ongoing testing every few years is a good practice.
